title: Class imbalance and stratified splitting, interactively
description: Course activity for Exercise 4: choose a class ratio and a predetermined split seed, then compare a stratified vs. an unstratified train/test split on the same resampled cohort of real ABIDE participants -- full-cohort and train/test class counts, confusion matrix, accuracy, AUC, and a majority-class baseline for each.
instructions: Choose a class ratio (control is always the majority class here) and one of five predetermined split seeds. Both panels use the exact same resampled cohort and the exact same model -- only whether the split preserved class proportions differs between them.
stratificationNote: Stratification preserves the resampled cohort's class proportions in both the training and test partitions; it does not create new minority-class observations, does not guarantee good sensitivity for the minority class, and does not change what the model's fitting objective optimizes for. At severe imbalance (95:5), compare each panel's accuracy against its own majority-class baseline: a classifier that predicts the majority class for everyone can still score a high accuracy while detecting no minority-class participants at all. Because each split is one stochastic draw, treat differences between the five seeds as examples of split-to-split stability, not proof that stratification must always score higher.
reflectionPrompts: At 95:5, compare accuracy to the majority-class baseline accuracy for both panels across all five seeds. How often does the model actually beat always-predict-control?

At 95:5, look at the unstratified panel's test-set minority count across the five seeds. How much does it vary, and what does that variation alone tell you about why an unstratified split is less reliable to evaluate?
Move from 50:50 down to 95:5. Does the STRATIFIED panel's train/test class proportion ever stop tracking the target ratio closely? Does the UNSTRATIFIED panel's?
